02 Accumulation & Wealth Building

The Waterfall

You've decided to save another dollar. Where it lands first can be worth tens of thousands by the time you retire.

The Planning LetterThe Contribution Order

Most savers get the hard part right and the easy part wrong. They summon the discipline to set money aside — the genuinely difficult act — and then drop it into whatever account is most familiar, usually the one their employer set up for them. The amount they save is admirable. The order in which they save it quietly leaves money on the table every year.

Think of your savings as water and your accounts as a series of basins arranged on a hillside. Water should fill the highest, most valuable basin completely before it spills into the next. Skip a basin out of habit, and you've poured a guaranteed return down the drain. This letter lays out that hillside — the contribution waterfall — in the order a dollar should actually flow.

Basin One

The match is not a perk. It's a 100% return.

If your employer matches contributions — say, 50 cents on the dollar up to 6% of pay — declining it is the single most expensive habit in personal finance. Put in a dollar, get fifty cents back the same day. That's an instant, risk-free 50% return before the market does anything at all. A dollar-for-dollar match is an instant 100%.

Compare that to the stock market's long-run average of roughly 7% real. The match isn't competing with the market — it's lapping it on day one. No legitimate investment offers a guaranteed 50% to 100% gain. This is why the match sits at the top of the hill, above even the celebrated HSA: leaving it unclaimed is the rare financial mistake with no upside whatsoever.

An unclaimed employer match is the only negative-return decision you can make while feeling responsible.

Basin Two

The HSA: the only triple-tax-free account in the code

If you're enrolled in a high-deductible health plan, the Health Savings Account is the most tax-advantaged vehicle in the entire tax code — and the most misunderstood. Most people treat it as a spending account for this year's copays. Treated instead as a stealth retirement account — invested, untouched, receipts saved — it does something no other account can: it dodges tax at all three gates.

2026 In Numbers

This year's basin sizes

The IRS raised nearly every limit for 2026. Here's how much each basin can hold — and the catch-up room if you're closing in on retirement.

Two honest caveats keep the waterfall from becoming dogma. First, the HSA only belongs in basin two if a high-deductible plan actually fits your health and family situation — never choose a worse insurance plan to chase a tax break. Second, if you carry high-interest debt, paying it off is its own basin near the very top: erasing 22% credit-card interest is a guaranteed 22% return, beating almost everything below it.

Today's Move

Map your savings against the hillside

Take your current monthly savings and trace where each dollar actually lands today.

  1. Write down every dollar you save monthly and which account it flows into right now.
  2. Confirm basin one is full: are you contributing at least enough to capture 100% of your employer match? If not, redirect there first.
  3. If you're on an HDHP and not maxing the HSA, route the next dollars there — and invest the balance rather than letting it sit in cash.
  4. Only after basins one and two are full should new money flow to Roth, then the rest of the 401(k), then taxable.
  5. Re-check in January each year — the basin sizes change with inflation, and 2026 raised most of them.

The discipline to save is the hard-won part, and if you've got it, you're already ahead of most. The waterfall simply makes sure that hard-won dollar lands where it earns the most — guaranteed returns before hoped-for ones, sheltered dollars before exposed ones. Same effort, materially more wealth.
